title: The Overcoat
author: Nikolai Gogol
setting: St Petersburg in Gogol’s own day: a government office, a tailor’s attic up a dark staircase, a superior’s flat in the fine part of town, an empty square at night and the Katinka Bridge
lengthNote: About 11,000 words in Claud Field’s translation, told straight through, with a single break before the ghost
openingLine: In a certain Russian ministerial department—
summary: A copying clerk in St Petersburg, mocked in his office and content with his desk, is told by his tailor that his old cloak cannot be patched again. He goes without tea and supper for months to pay for a new one, wears it for one day, and has it stolen on the way home from a party. The official he asks for help shouts at him, he dies of a fever within the week, and then a ghost starts pulling the cloaks off the backs of Petersburg’s officials. Gogol tells it through a talkative, forgetful narrator, so that the reader is never sure whether to laugh at Akaki or pity him, and readers have argued in those terms ever since.
referenceStyle: episode of the story, named as in the plot outline; Field’s translation has no numbered parts, only one break before the ghost

sourceText.label: Project Gutenberg text of The Mantle and Other Stories, translated by Claud Field (eBook 36238)
sourceText.note: Field’s translation of 1916, which the Astor edition prints under the title The Overcoat. Field calls the garment a cloak and sometimes a mantle, and spells the names his own way: Akaki Akakievitch Bashmatchkin, Petrovitch, the Katinka Bridge (the Kalinkin Bridge) and the Obuchoff Bridge (the Obukhov). He gives the title Superintendent both to the district police officer Akaki visits first and to the important personage he visits second; they are two different men. Quotations follow Field’s wording exactly.

atAGlance.label: Begun
atAGlance.note: Mikhail Pogodin took down a first draft from Gogol’s dictation at Marienbad that July, under the working title A Tale of a Clerk Who Steals Overcoats.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: In the third volume of Gogol’s collected Works, printed at the end of 1842 and held back by the censor until January 1843.

atAGlance.label: The hero’s grade
atAGlance.note: The ninth of the fourteen civil grades in Peter the Great’s Table of Ranks. Field calls him a permanent titular councillor: he will never rise.

atAGlance.label: This translation
atAGlance.note: From The Mantle and Other Stories, published in London by T. Werner Laurie with Prosper Mérimée’s essay on Gogol as a preface.

structure.label: The copyist
structure.title: A clerk, his name and his desk
structure.summary: The narrator will not name the department, describes a short, pock-marked, balding titular councillor, and explains how he came to be called Akaki Akakievitch. Nobody in the office notices him except to tease him. He loves copying, cannot manage any other task, copies at home for pleasure and asks nothing more of life than four hundred roubles a year.

scenes.title: A department not named
scenes.summary: Touchy officials, a provincial magistrate’s complaint about a novel, and a hero produced by the Petersburg climate.

scenes.title: Names from the calendar
scenes.summary: Mokuja, Triphiliy, Pavsikakhiy: his mother gives up on the saints and names him after his father.

scenes.title: Paper snowflakes
scenes.summary: The clerks’ jokes, his one protest, and the young clerk who hears it for the rest of his life.

scenes.title: A world of varied beauty
scenes.summary: His favourite letters, the report he cannot redraft, his faded uniform and his evenings at home.

structure.label: The old cloak
structure.title: Petrovitch’s verdict
structure.summary: The winter cold finds the holes in his cloak, which the office calls a cowl. Petrovitch the tailor, sober and therefore stubborn, will not patch it again and names a price of a hundred and fifty roubles. A Sunday visit and a ten-kopeck piece change nothing. Akaki gives up tea, supper and the fire in his own room to save, the thought of the new cloak becomes his companion, and an unusually large bonus brings the day forward.

scenes.title: The northern cold
scenes.summary: Four hundred roubles a year against a Petersburg winter, and a cloak worn so thin that the light shows through.

scenes.title: The tailor’s attic
scenes.summary: Fish frying, a snuff-box general with a paper face, and the verdict that the old cloak is a wretched rag.

scenes.title: Months of going without
scenes.summary: Forty roubles already saved a kopeck at a time, the rest found by going hungry, and monthly visits to talk over the cloth.

scenes.title: Buying the cloth
scenes.summary: A bonus of sixty-five roubles, good cloth, a glossy linen lining, and catskin in place of marten.

structure.label: The new cloak
structure.title: One day in a new cloak
structure.summary: Petrovitch delivers the cloak on a frosty morning. The office crowds round to admire it and demands a celebration, and a superior with a birthday invites them all to tea instead. Akaki walks to the fine quarter, sits out the card games, drinks two glasses of champagne and slips away after midnight. Crossing an enormous empty square on the way home he is knocked down and robbed, and the sentry says he thought the men were his friends.

scenes.title: Warm and beautiful
scenes.summary: The tailor lays it on his shoulders, follows him into the street, and the whole office comes to look.

scenes.title: Tea in the fine quarter
scenes.summary: Galoshes in the hall, whist, cold veal and champagne, and the cloak found lying on the floor.

scenes.title: The empty square
scenes.summary: A long dark street, a square like a desert, men with long moustaches, and a sentry who saw nothing wrong.

structure.label: The petition
structure.title: Two officials and a fever
structure.summary: His landlady sends him to the district superintendent, who wants to know why he was out so late. The office takes up a collection that raises almost nothing. On a colleague’s advice he goes to an important personage, who keeps him waiting to impress an old friend and then shouts at him until he has to be dragged out. Akaki walks home through a storm, catches a fever and dies within days; the office learns of it four days after the funeral.

scenes.title: A police officer’s questions
scenes.summary: Three calls before he is admitted, and questions about suspicious company where there should be questions about the theft.

scenes.title: Severity
scenes.summary: A new official, a visiting friend, a practised stern voice, and a petitioner carried half-conscious down the stairs.

scenes.title: Goose-quills and socks
scenes.summary: Delirium, a doctor who prices the coffin, an estate of a few belongings, and a successor of robuster fibre.

structure.label: The ghost
structure.title: The ghost at the Katinka Bridge
structure.summary: A dead clerk begins pulling cloaks off passers-by near the Katinka Bridge; the police catch him once and lose him in a sneeze. The important personage, who has felt a pang on hearing of Akaki’s death, is seized by the collar on his way home from a party and hands over his own cloak. After that the ghost is not seen, unless it is the taller shadow with an enormous moustache that a nervous sentry follows towards the Obuchoff Bridge.

scenes.title: The rumour
scenes.summary: Cloaks of every fur taken without regard to rank, colds in honourable backs, and a sentry’s snuff.

scenes.title: The important personage’s cloak
scenes.summary: A pleasant evening, two glasses of champagne, a hand on the collar in the sledge, and a changed manner afterwards.

scenes.title: A taller shadow
scenes.summary: A sentry follows a figure with an enormous moustache, is shouted at, and lets it go.

characters.name: Akaki Akakievitch Bashmatchkin
characters.summary: A clerk in his fifties who has copied documents in the same chancellery for as long as anyone can remember. He loves the letters he forms, eats without tasting, cannot finish a sentence and asks nothing of anybody except to be left to work. The new cloak gives him, for the first time, something to want, and wanting changes him: he saves, plans, walks faster and even dreams of a marten collar. After the theft he speaks up once, is shouted down and dies. As a ghost he becomes the only version of himself that anyone fears.
characters.clue: He copies letters to important people at home in the evenings for pleasure, and when given a report to redraft he begs to be given something to copy instead.

characters.name: Petrovitch
characters.role: Tailor, once a serf, one-eyed and fond of brandy
characters.summary: Once a serf called Gregor, he took a new name when he was freed and began to drink on every holy day in the calendar. He is sharp, proud of his trade and pleased to name a price that makes a customer flinch. He also makes the best thing that ever happens to Akaki: he spends a fortnight on the cloak, sews it all with silk, charges twelve roubles and follows it down the street to watch it being worn.
characters.clue: A one-eyed craftsman with a thumbnail like a tortoise shell, who tells a customer to cut his rag up into foot bandages because the Germans invented stockings.

characters.name: The important personage
characters.role: A newly promoted official, whom Field also calls the Superintendent
characters.summary: Gogol never gives him a name or a post that can be pinned down. He has recently been promoted, has practised his stern voice in front of a looking-glass, and runs his ten subordinates on a single word, severity. Among men of his own rank he is pleasant; below it he freezes, and he knows he is missing something. He shouts at Akaki mainly to impress an old friend, feels a pang when he hears of the death, and changes his manner only after the ghost has taken his cloak.
characters.clue: After his promotion he spent eight days rehearsing a stern tone in front of a mirror, and he uses it on a petitioner to impress a visitor from the country.

characters.name: The young clerk
characters.role: A newcomer who joins the teasing once
characters.summary: He appears in one paragraph and matters out of all proportion. Something in Akaki’s voice stops him in the middle of a practical joke, and for years afterwards, in cheerful company, he hears the plea to be left alone and, behind it, a question about brotherhood. He is the only person whose view of Akaki changes while Akaki is alive, and the story’s few lines of open pity come to the reader through him.
characters.clue: Years later, among cheerful friends, he hides his face in his hands at the memory of a voice asking to be left alone.

characters.name: The clerks of the chancellery
characters.summary: They drop paper snow on his head, invent stories about his landlady and demand a feast when he arrives in a new cloak. When he is robbed some of them laugh; most are sorry and take up a collection, which raises very little because they have just paid for their director’s portrait. They hear of his death four days after he is buried, and his desk is filled the next day.
characters.clue: They told a man that the scraps of paper falling on his head were snow, and later could spare him very little because they had just bought their director’s portrait.

characters.name: The landlady
characters.summary: The clerks joke that she beats him and ask when he will marry her. She lets him copy in her room so that he can save the fuel in his own, sends him to the district superintendent she knows through her former cook, sits by him in his fever and crosses herself at the titles he calls out in delirium.
characters.clue: At seventy she lets her lodger work in her room to save his firewood, and is frightened when he keeps crying Your Excellency in a fever.

characters.name: The thieves
characters.role: The men with long moustaches in the square
characters.summary: Several men whose faces Akaki cannot make out. One says the cloak is his and takes him by the collar, another holds a bony fist over his mouth, and by the time Akaki comes round in the snow they are gone. The story never finds them. At the very end a figure with an enormous moustache, taller than Akaki’s ghost, turns on a sentry and strides off into the dark, which leaves open whether the last ghost in the story is one of them.
characters.clue: One of them claims a stranger’s garment as his own while tearing it off him in the middle of an empty square.

characters.name: The narrator
characters.role: The talkative teller of the story
characters.summary: He will not name the department, forgets where the party was, does not know who got Akaki’s belongings and admits he has never asked. He passes from comedy to sentiment and back inside a paragraph, and his asides about officials are funny partly because he shares their habits. Boris Eikhenbaum’s essay of 1919 put him at the centre of the story: in that reading the voice, with its jokes and lapses, decides how a reader feels about Akaki.
characters.clue: He cannot remember which street the tea party was in, and says he has never inquired who inherited a dead man’s goose-quills.

themes.name: Rank
themes.summary: The narrator gives Akaki’s grade before his name, because in Russia, he says, rank must always be given. Everyone in the story knows where they stand. The clerks mock the man below them, the important personage performs severity for the men below him, and the titular councillor who calls his tiny office a Council-chamber copies the manners of his betters. The only figure who ignores the ladder is a ghost, who strips cloaks from clerks and state councillors alike.
themes.development: A permanent titular councillor on the first page; porters who do not stand up for him; a question put three times, Do you know with whom you are speaking?; a ghost who pays no attention to rank or title.

themes.name: The cloak
themes.summary: Clothes show rank in this story, and a cloak is the nearest thing Akaki has to a companion. The old one has been patched with pieces of its own collar until the office calls it a cowl; the new one has catskin where the cloaks of better men have marten; the cloaks in a superior’s hall hang in rows with fur collars. The narrator compares the thought of the new cloak to a wife. Losing it kills Akaki, and as a ghost his only demand is for a cloak.
themes.development: Holes you can see through; a hundred and fifty roubles quoted, eighty found; twelve roubles for the tailoring; one day of wearing it; then furs of every kind taken near the Katinka Bridge.

themes.name: Copying
themes.summary: Akaki’s happiness is copying. He has favourite letters, smiles when he reaches them, takes documents home and copies letters to important people for his own satisfaction. Offered something more responsible, turning a report from the first person into the third, he sweats and begs to go back. Gogol makes the lowest work in the office a kind of art and the whole of a man’s life, and when Akaki dies his place is taken the next day by an official who does not bother with so many fair copies.
themes.development: Copying at the office, copying at home, copying at the landlady’s table to save fuel; a slip of the pen when the cloak fills his head; a bundle of goose-quills left behind.

themes.name: Pity and mockery
themes.summary: The office laughs at Akaki and the narrator often laughs with it. One paragraph goes the other way: a young clerk hears in Akaki’s voice the words Am I not your brother? and hides his face at the memory years later. Readers have divided over which of these the story means. Critics in the 1840s read it as a plea for the poor clerk, and Dostoevsky’s first novel answered it in those terms; in 1919 Boris Eikhenbaum argued that the humane paragraph is one more voice in a comic performance. Both responses can be supported from the text.
themes.development: Paper snowflakes; the young clerk’s memory; a collection that raises almost nothing; some colleagues laughing and most sorry; the important personage’s pang of conscience.

themes.name: Money
themes.summary: Every sum is exact. A salary of four hundred roubles; a Christmas bonus of forty or fifty in an ordinary year and sixty-five in this one; a kopeck put by from every rouble until the box holds forty; eighty roubles in the end, and a charge of twelve for the tailoring. Akaki gives up evening tea, supper and his own fire to find the difference, and walks carefully to save his shoes. The cost of one coat is the plot, and the careful accounting is part of the comedy and part of the sorrow.
themes.development: Four hundred roubles on the first page of the misfortune; a hundred and fifty named in the attic; the kopeck box; the bonus; a doctor who orders pine because oak would be too dear.

themes.name: St Petersburg
themes.summary: Petersburg is a climate first. The narrator says Akaki’s face was produced by it, the northern cold is every poor clerk’s enemy, and the wind in the narrow streets gives him the illness that kills him. It is also a map of rank, from staircases reeking of spirits to lamp-lit streets full of lacquered sleighs and bearskins, and at night it becomes a desert of a square with a sentry-box at the end of the world. When Akaki dies, the great city carries on as though he had never existed.
themes.development: A grey northern sky; tailors on the Nevski Prospect who would charge sixty-five roubles; the smart quarter where the superior lives; the Katinka and Obuchoff bridges, both real bridges over the Fontanka.

themes.name: The ghost
themes.summary: In the last pages the story becomes a Petersburg legend. A dead clerk pulls cloaks off passers-by near the Katinka Bridge, escapes arrest in a sneeze, and stops only when he has the important personage’s cloak. The narrator calls his tale fantastic yet veracious, and then reopens his own ending with a second, taller ghost wearing a moustache. The ghost can be read as justice, as a joke about rumour, or as the city’s bad conscience, and the text leaves room for each.
themes.development: A rumour, a sighting by a former colleague, a sentry’s snuff, the personage’s collar seized in his sledge, and a shadow walking towards the Obuchoff Bridge.

techniques.name: The intruding narrator
techniques.definition: A narrator who interrupts the story to comment, digress or talk about the telling.
techniques.inThisBook: He declines to name the department in case officials take offence, admits his memory is failing, stops to tell anecdotes about a council-chamber in a cupboard of an office, and closes Akaki’s life with a shrug about who got his things. The interruptions keep the reader at a comic distance from the clerk, which makes the few moments of plain pity stand out.

techniques.name: Skaz
techniques.definition: Russian term for narration written to sound like a particular speaker telling the story aloud, with his own habits, errors and asides.
techniques.inThisBook: Gogol’s teller hedges (if I am not mistaken), loses his thread and gives small things grand words. Boris Eikhenbaum used The Overcoat in 1919 to show how such a voice can decide the shape of a whole story. In Field’s English the effect survives in the asides and the mock-solemn phrasing; the puns and sound-play that depend on Russian mostly do not.

techniques.name: The comic grotesque
techniques.definition: Exaggerated, often physical detail that makes a person or thing ridiculous and strange together.
techniques.inThisBook: A neck stretched like the toy cats with movable heads sold on trays in villages, a tailor’s thumbnail as hard as a tortoise shell, a general on a snuff-box whose face has been patched with paper, orange peel on a hat. The details belittle, and Gogol’s reader has to look for the man behind them.

techniques.name: Symbolic names
techniques.definition: Names chosen for their meaning or their sound.
techniques.inThisBook: Akaki is given his father’s name twice over after a page of real but outlandish saints’ names from the church calendar. The name goes back to a Greek word for guileless, and the surname Bashmatchkin comes from the Russian for a shoe, a joke Field’s translation leaves out. A man who is given nothing of his own is not even given a name of his own.

techniques.name: Irony
techniques.definition: Saying one thing in words whose real meaning is different, or letting events contradict what characters expect.
techniques.inThisBook: The thief shouts That is my cloak!; the important personage scolds a man in his fifties for the rebelliousness of the young; the collection for the robbed man fails because the office has just paid for its director’s portrait; the man best placed to help is the one busiest impressing his friend.

techniques.name: Shifts of register
techniques.definition: Movement between different levels or kinds of language, such as the comic and the solemn.
techniques.inThisBook: Without warning the story moves from farce to pathos and back: the paper-snowflake joke is followed by the young clerk’s shame, the doctor’s pine coffin by a sentence about the city going on as though Akaki had never existed. Readers disagree about which register has the last word.

techniques.name: Comic repetition
techniques.definition: A word, phrase or action repeated until it becomes a joke or a mark of character.
techniques.inThisBook: Severity said three times in succession; Do you consider before whom you are standing? asked and asked again; Akaki’s Yes—it is indeed true that— which never reaches its end. The important personage’s catch-phrase returns after the ghost as the thing he no longer says.

techniques.name: Inventory
techniques.definition: A list of things that stands in for a description of a person or a life.
techniques.inThisBook: Akaki’s estate is a bundle of goose-quills, a notebook of white paper, three pairs of socks, some trouser buttons and the old coat. The ghost takes cloaks lined with wadding, mink, cat, otter, bear or beaverskin. The first list is the whole of one life; the second sorts the city by the fur it can afford.

techniques.name: The open ending
techniques.definition: An ending that leaves the central question unanswered.
techniques.inThisBook: The ghost stops appearing once it has the important personage’s cloak, which reads like a moral ending, and then a taller figure with a moustache is seen walking off into the dark. The last paragraph points back to the thieves and away from any settled meaning.

quotations.text: But it is perhaps better that I do not mention which department it was. There are in the whole of Russia no persons more sensitive than Government officials.
quotations.context: The narrator breaks off his first sentence before he has named the department.
quotations.analysis: Before the story has properly begun, the narrator loses his nerve. He stops mid-sentence to avoid offending the class the story is about to expose, and his joke about touchy officials, one of whom sent in a whole novel as evidence of an insult, is also a joke about censorship under Nicholas I. From the first lines the reader knows this teller is timid, chatty and not quite in charge of his material.

quotations.text: Such was the outer aspect of our hero, as produced by the St Petersburg climate.
quotations.context: After a description of Akaki’s short stature, pock-marked face and bald forehead.
quotations.analysis: Gogol blames the weather for the man. The line is a comic shrug, but it sets up the logic of the whole story: the northern cold wears out the old cloak, makes a new one necessary, and finally sends the wind that gives Akaki his fatal fever. The city makes him and then disposes of him.

quotations.text: As regards his official rank—for with us Russians the official rank must always be given—he was what is usually known as a permanent titular councillor
quotations.context: The hero’s rank is given before his name.
quotations.analysis: A man is his grade in this society, and a description that left the grade out would be incomplete. Titular councillor was the ninth of fourteen civil grades in Peter the Great’s Table of Ranks, and permanent means he will never rise from it. The narrator mocks the custom in the same breath as he obeys it.

quotations.text: It was baptised, although it wept and cried and made all kinds of grimaces, as though it had a presentiment that it would one day be a titular councillor.
quotations.context: His mother, rejecting a string of outlandish saints’ names from the church calendar, has settled on his father’s name.
quotations.analysis: Gogol calls the baby it, and has him howl at his future grade. After a page of absurd calendar names he ends up with his father’s name twice, Akaki son of Akaki, as if nothing of his own could be found for him. The joke about fate is also the story’s plan, since he is born into the rank he will die in.

quotations.text: Even the office attendants did not rise from their seats when he entered, nor look at him; they took no more notice than if a fly had flown through the room.
quotations.context: How the chancellery treats him.
quotations.analysis: Even the attendants, the lowest people in the building, can look down on him. The comparison with a fly is precise about what he is to them, something that moves without mattering. Gogol returns to insects after Akaki’s death, when the narrator remarks that he never roused the curiosity even of the naturalists, who are eager to put a rare insect under the microscope.

quotations.text: Sometimes they let a shower of scraps of paper fall on his head, and told him they were snowflakes.
quotations.context: The young clerks’ games at Akaki’s expense.
quotations.analysis: Childish and cruel, the joke is made of paper, the material of his whole working life. It also brings winter indoors. Real Petersburg snow will soon matter more to Akaki than anything in the office, and the story’s weather begins here as a prank.

quotations.text: Do leave me alone! Why do you always want to disturb me at work?
quotations.speaker: Akaki Akakievitch
quotations.context: His only protest, made when the clerks hold his arm to stop him writing.
quotations.analysis: It is barely a protest. He accuses nobody, and even now what matters to him is the work. The narrator says there was something peculiarly pathetic in the words and the way they were spoken, and they are the words that follow the young clerk for the rest of his life. Akaki’s whole defence of himself is to ask to be allowed to copy.

quotations.text: Along with these words, he also heard others: “Am I not your brother?”
quotations.context: A new clerk has been stopped in the middle of a practical joke by something in Akaki’s voice; years later he still hears it.
quotations.analysis: Akaki never says this. The young clerk hears it behind the words he did say, and it sounds like scripture. Field makes it a question, where Gogol’s Russian is a plain statement, I am your brother, and the question has the tone of an appeal. For many readers this paragraph is the moral centre of the story; for others, following Boris Eikhenbaum, it is one more change of voice in a comic performance.

quotations.text: While he copied official documents, a world of varied beauty rose before his eyes.
quotations.context: The narrator corrects himself: zealously is too weak a word for how Akaki works.
quotations.analysis: Nobody else in the story loves anything the way Akaki loves the shapes of letters. He has favourites, smiles when he reaches them, and his face shows which letter he is forming. The sentence is half a joke about a clerk’s narrow pleasures and half a portrait of an artist, and it is the happiest thing the narrator ever says about him.

quotations.text: No! Please give me again something to copy.
quotations.speaker: Akaki Akakievitch
quotations.context: A kindly director has given him a more important task: redrafting a report, altering headings and changing the first person into the third.
quotations.analysis: His one chance of promotion fails because he cannot bear to alter anything. The task itself is a quiet joke, shifting I to he, the grammar by which a person becomes a case in a file. He sweats, begs to go back, and the office lets him copy for the rest of his life.

quotations.text: The collar was so narrow and so tight that his neck, although of average length, stretched far out of it, and appeared extraordinarily long, just like those of the cats with movable heads, which are carried about on trays and sold to the peasants in Russian villages.
quotations.context: His uniform, once green, has faded to a reddish colour.
quotations.analysis: With this simile he shrinks to a cheap toy, the nodding cat on a village pedlar’s tray. Gogol builds the portrait from clothes: the uniform has changed colour, the collar pinches, rubbish sticks to his hat. Before the cloak enters the story the reader already knows that in this world a man is seen through what he wears.

quotations.text: In St Petersburg all those who draw a salary of four hundred roubles or thereabouts have a terrible enemy in our northern cold, although some assert that it is very good for the health.
quotations.context: The narrator turns from Akaki’s contentment to the misfortune that ends it.
quotations.analysis: Cold is sorted by income here. A salary figure opens the sentence as if the weather read pay slips, and the last clause, about the cold being healthy, is what comfortable people say. From here the story is about the arithmetic of keeping warm on four hundred roubles a year.

quotations.text: No, it won’t bear anything more; cloth after all is only cloth, and in its present condition a gust of wind might blow the wretched mantle into tatters.
quotations.speaker: Petrovitch
quotations.context: Akaki pleads for one more repair.
quotations.analysis: Petrovitch speaks as a craftsman and enjoys it: the material has a limit, and he is the one who knows where it is. His verdict also condemns Akaki’s whole way of life, which has been to mend, patch and go without. The narrator describes the tailor’s firmness as a brave defence of the art of tailoring, and it is what sets the story moving.

quotations.text: “A hundred and fifty roubles for a cloak!” exclaimed Akaki Akakievitch in a tone which sounded like an outcry—possibly the first he had uttered since his birth.
quotations.speaker: Akaki Akakievitch
quotations.context: Petrovitch names his price, and adds that a marten collar and a silk-lined hood would bring it to two hundred.
quotations.analysis: A man whose sentences usually dissolve into particles finally raises his voice, and the subject is money. The narrator’s aside, possibly the first cry since his birth, makes the moment comic and sad together. The figure explains the shout: it is more than a third of his salary for a year.

quotations.text: From that time it seemed as though his nature had completed itself; as though he had married and possessed a companion on his life journey. This companion was the thought of his new cloak, properly wadded and lined.
quotations.context: He has given up tea, supper and the fire in his own room to save the money.
quotations.analysis: Gogol gives Akaki a marriage and makes the bride the idea of a coat. It is the story’s central image, and the sentence is funny because it is so exactly observed: the saving, the planning and the monthly visits to Petrovitch really are a courtship. The loss that follows is a bereavement, and the story treats it as one.
quotations.source: Field translation, saving for the cloak

quotations.text: He was fully conscious of his dignity, and of the gulf which separates the tailor who only repairs old clothes from the artist who makes new ones.
quotations.context: Petrovitch arrives early in the morning with the finished cloak wrapped in a clean handkerchief.
quotations.analysis: Petrovitch has his own Table of Ranks, and today he has been promoted. The mock-solemn word artist is only partly a joke. He has made something fine, he charges less than a Nevski Prospect tailor would, and he follows Akaki down the street to watch it being worn. Gogol gives the craftsman the one uncomplicated pride in the story.

quotations.text: At a great distance—God knows where!—glimmered the light in a sentry-box, which seemed to stand at the end of the world.
quotations.context: Walking home after midnight from the party, he comes out into an enormous square.
quotations.analysis: Here the comic city of offices and tailors gives way to emptiness. The sentry-box, where help ought to be, is so far off that it seems to belong to another world, and the sentry says a moment later that he saw the men and took them for friends. Akaki keeps his eyes on the ground so as not to see the expanse, and when he raises them the thieves are there.

quotations.text: “That is my cloak!” shouted one of the men, and seized him by the collar.
quotations.speaker: The thieves
quotations.context: Several men with long moustaches step out of the dark in the middle of the square.
quotations.analysis: Whose cloak is it? The thief claims it, and in a sense everyone has: the office wanted it celebrated, the party wanted it admired, and now the street takes it. The words make ownership a matter of who shouts first. They return at the end, spoken the other way round, when Akaki’s ghost seizes another man by the collar and demands his cloak.

quotations.text: Instead of confining himself to the principal matter—the theft, he asked the titular councillor how he came to be out so late, and whether he had not been in suspicious company.
quotations.context: Akaki has forced his way in to see the police officer his landlady recommended.
quotations.analysis: In this office the victim is treated as the suspect. It is the first of Akaki’s two interviews with authority and it prepares the second, in which the official again cares about procedure and respectability and puts his questions to the petitioner. He leaves not knowing whether anything will be done, and the cloak is never found.

quotations.text: His system might be summed up in a single word—“severity.”
quotations.context: The narrator describes the man Akaki has been advised to approach.
quotations.analysis: Severity is his entire method, and he says the word three times in succession, turning a piercing look on his listener at the third. The narrator adds that his ten subordinates were frightened enough already. The man is a caricature of a new official rehearsing authority, and the comedy of the rehearsal explains why his cruelty to Akaki is so casual.

quotations.text: “Do you also know,” he continued, “with whom you are speaking? Do you consider before whom you are standing? Do you consider, I ask you, do you consider?”
quotations.speaker: The important personage
quotations.context: Akaki has just said that secretaries are a hopeless kind of people.
quotations.analysis: Each question answers itself, since the answer is always the speaker. He stamps his foot as his voice grows deeper, and glances at his friend to see the effect. Akaki has to be dragged out almost unconscious. The speech is the story’s clearest picture of rank as performance, delivered in a voice practised before a looking-glass for eight days.

quotations.text: Allow me to remark to Your Excellence that I ventured to trouble you personally in this matter because secretaries—secretaries are a hopeless kind of people.
quotations.speaker: Akaki Akakievitch
quotations.context: Sweating, he tries to explain why he has not gone through the proper channels.
quotations.analysis: This is the nearest Akaki comes to rebellion, and it slips out. His stammer catches on the word secretaries as if he were surprised to hear himself say it. The important personage hears insubordination and lectures a man in his fifties on the rebelliousness of the young. The one opinion Akaki ever offers is punished on the spot.

quotations.text: He had no heir and left nothing behind him but a bundle of goose-quills, a notebook of white paper, three pairs of socks, some trouser buttons, and his old coat.
quotations.context: Why nobody came to seal up his room.
quotations.analysis: Everything he owned fits into one sentence: the tools of copying, unused paper and a few clothes. The old coat outlasts its owner. The narrator follows the list by wondering who got these relics and admitting that he has never inquired, so that even the dead man’s estate attracts no curiosity.

quotations.text: The great city of St Petersburg continued its life as though he had never existed.
quotations.context: After his burial.
quotations.analysis: After pages of jokes this sentence is plain, and the plainness gives it force. It could close the story. The next paragraphs add that the office heard of the death four days late and filled his seat the next morning with an official of robuster fibre, which makes the same observation comic again.

quotations.text: It mattered not whether they were lined with wadding, mink, cat, otter, bear, or beaverskin; he took all he could get hold of.
quotations.context: The rumour of a ghost in a chancellery uniform near the Katinka Bridge.
quotations.analysis: Each lining in the list belongs to a rank, from the wadding a clerk might afford to the beaver of a senior man, and the ghost treats them alike. The clerk who could not stretch to marten now takes everyone’s collar, and state councillors catch colds in their honourable backs. The revenge is levelling, and it is also a joke about the city’s appetite for rumour.

quotations.text: At last I have you—by the collar! I need your cloak. You did not trouble about me when I was in distress; you thought it necessary to reprimand me. Now give me your cloak.
quotations.speaker: Akaki Akakievitch
quotations.context: The important personage, riding home in his sledge after a cheerful evening, feels a hand on his collar.
quotations.analysis: Dead, the man who could never finish a sentence speaks in complete, accusing ones. The words repeat the thief’s act in the square, the grip on the collar, and they make the charge the living Akaki never could: you did not trouble about me. The important personage hands over his cloak with a trembling hand and tells the coachman to drive home.

quotations.text: This shadow, however, was taller than the ghost of the titular councillor, and had an enormous moustache.
quotations.context: A nervous sentry has followed a shadow, which turned, shook an enormous fist and shouted at him.
quotations.analysis: Just as the story settles into justice done, a second figure appears, taller, with the moustache of the men in the square, striding towards the Obuchoff Bridge. It may be one of the thieves, another ghost or a timid sentry’s fancy. The narrator does not say, and the story stops.

timeline.label: Peter the Great introduces the Table of Ranks
timeline.detail: Fourteen grades each for the army, the navy and the civil service, with promotion meant to depend on service. A titular councillor stood in the ninth civil grade.

timeline.label: Nikolai Gogol is born at Sorochyntsi, in the Poltava province of the Russian Empire, now Ukraine
timeline.detail: He grew up on his family’s small estate and went to school at Nizhyn.

timeline.label: Gogol takes a clerk’s post in St Petersburg
timeline.detail: Until 1831 he served in minor posts in the Department of State Economy and Public Buildings and then the Department of Appanages, the world of the copying clerk.

timeline.label: Around this time Gogol hears the story of a clerk and his gun
timeline.detail: As P. V. Annenkov recalled it, a poor clerk saved for months to buy a fine gun and lost it from his boat on his first day’s shooting; he fell ill with grief, and his colleagues bought him another.

timeline.label: Arabesques includes Nevsky Prospect, The Portrait and Diary of a Madman
timeline.detail: The first of the stories later grouped as Gogol’s Petersburg tales.

timeline.label: The Nose appears, The Government Inspector is staged, and Gogol leaves Russia
timeline.detail: He spent most of the next twelve years abroad, much of it in Rome.

timeline.label: Pogodin takes down a first draft at Marienbad
timeline.detail: Gogol dictated it in July under the working title A Tale of a Clerk Who Steals Overcoats.

timeline.label: The Overcoat is printed in the third volume of Gogol’s Works
timeline.detail: The volume was printed at the end of the year and went on sale in January 1843 after a delay at the censor. The first part of Dead Souls had appeared that spring.

timeline.label: Dostoevsky’s Poor Folk
timeline.detail: In his first novel the poor clerk Makar Devushkin reads The Overcoat and is hurt by it, because he recognises himself.

timeline.label: Gogol dies in Moscow
timeline.detail: On 4 March 1852, 21 February in the Russian calendar of the time, days after burning the manuscript of the second part of Dead Souls.

timeline.label: Vogüé prints the saying about Gogol’s overcoat
timeline.detail: In Le Roman russe the French critic Eugène-Melchior de Vogüé credits an unnamed Russian with the words We have all come out of Gogol’s Overcoat. It is often given to Dostoevsky, without evidence.

timeline.label: Claud Field’s translation, The Mantle and Other Stories
timeline.detail: Published in London by T. Werner Laurie and in New York by Frederick A. Stokes, with The Nose, Memoirs of a Madman, A May Night and The Viy.

timeline.label: Boris Eikhenbaum’s essay How Gogol’s Overcoat Is Made
timeline.detail: A founding text of Russian Formalist criticism, which reads the story through its narrator’s voice.

timeline.label: Grigori Kozintsev and Leonid Trauberg film The Overcoat
timeline.detail: A silent film made in Leningrad, with a script by Yury Tynyanov that draws on Nevsky Prospect as well.

places.name: Nevsky Prospect, St Petersburg
places.note: The city’s main street, where, Petrovitch says, a tailor would have charged at least sixty-five roubles for the same work.

places.name: Kalinkin Bridge, St Petersburg
places.note: Field’s Katinka Bridge over the Fontanka, near which the ghost first starts taking cloaks.

places.name: Obukhov Bridge, St Petersburg
places.note: Field’s Obuchoff Bridge, towards which the last shadow with the enormous moustache strides off.

places.name: Marienbad (Mariánské Lázně)
places.note: The spa town where Mikhail Pogodin took down the first draft from Gogol’s dictation in July 1839.

places.name: Via Sistina, Rome
places.note: Gogol lodged here during his Roman years, when much of the story was written.

criticalViews.position: A plea for the little man
criticalViews.summary: The reading that took hold in Russia in the 1840s: Akaki is the first of literature’s downtrodden clerks, the office and the important personage stand for a heartless bureaucracy, and the young clerk’s paragraph about brotherhood is the story’s moral centre. Dostoevsky’s Poor Folk and a flood of stories about poor officials took the story in this spirit.
criticalViews.counter: The paragraph is one of very few, and the narrator spends far more time laughing at Akaki than weeping for him. By 1861 the radical critic Chernyshevsky was complaining that sentimental pity for such figures had had its day and that Akaki was simply a fool, and the ghost’s revenge is played for laughs as much as for justice.

criticalViews.summary: Boris Eikhenbaum’s essay of 1919 argues that the story is organised by its narrator’s voice, a spoken performance of puns, digressions and sudden changes of tone, and that the humane paragraph is a deliberate switch into declamation inside that performance. On this view the reader who weeps has been played on.
criticalViews.counter: A reading that attends only to style has trouble with the exactness of the sums, the ranks and the city, which are social observation of a precise kind. It also has to explain why so many readers, in Russian and in translation, have felt the pity as real.

criticalViews.position: A saint’s life turned upside down
criticalViews.summary: Some critics read Akaki through the lives of the saints. His name is a saint’s name, his copying is like a monk’s obedience, his fast for the cloak is a kind of asceticism, and his return from the grave reverses the miracles of a holy life. The story becomes a parody of hagiography, or a religious fable about poverty of spirit.
criticalViews.counter: The saintly details sit next to haemorrhoids, orange peel and a thief’s moustache, and the ghost is a robber. If the pattern is there, Gogol handles it so comically that it is hard to say whether he is honouring the saint or mocking the reader who looks for one.

essayQuestions.question: Is The Overcoat a comic story or a tragic one?
essayQuestions.focus: Tone, the narrator and the reader’s sympathy
plan: Begin with the narrator: the department he will not name, the memory that fails, the jokes about officials. Show how he keeps Akaki at a distance.

Set the comic grotesque, the toy cats, the paper snowflakes, the tailor’s thumbnail, against the plain moments of feeling: the young clerk’s memory and the city carrying on as though Akaki had never existed.
Read the cloak as companion closely: the comedy of the comparison and the grief it prepares.
Weigh the two famous readings, the plea for the little man and Eikhenbaum’s comic performance, using the paragraph about brotherhood.
End with the ghost and the taller shadow with a moustache, and what they do to the reader’s final feeling.

essayQuestions.question: How does Gogol present rank and authority in The Overcoat?
essayQuestions.focus: The Table of Ranks, the office and the two interviews
plan: Start from the aside that rank must always be given, and the permanent titular councillor.
Map the office: attendants who ignore him, clerks who mock him, a director who gives bonuses and is given his portrait.
Compare the two interviews: the district superintendent’s questions and the important personage’s rehearsed severity.
Show how everyone copies the rank above: Petrovitch’s pride as an artist, the titular councillor’s Council-chamber.
Finish with the ghost who ignores rank, and the important personage’s partial change.

essayQuestions.question: What does the cloak mean to Akaki, and why does its loss destroy him?
plan: The old cloak called a cowl: clothes as the office’s measure of a man.
The saving: the exact sums, the tea and suppers given up, the thought of the cloak as a companion.
The day of the cloak: warm and beautiful, the office’s attention, the party in the fine quarter.
The theft and the petitions: what he loses is also the first attention he has ever received.
The ghost’s demand for a cloak and the personage’s cloak handed over: does the ending satisfy his desire or make fun of it?

discussionQuestions: The narrator cannot remember where the party was and has never asked who got Akaki’s belongings. Why give the story such a careless teller?
Akaki never says Am I not your brother? Whose words are they, and why does Gogol put them in someone else’s memory?
Is Petrovitch a villain, an artist or both?
The important personage feels a pang of conscience before the ghost appears. Does the story forgive him?
What would be lost if the story ended with Akaki’s burial?
Why might Gogol give the last figure in the story a moustache?

related.why: Dostoevsky’s Petersburg official of twenty years later, who knows everything about his own humiliation that Akaki never notices, and talks of little else.
Tolstoy’s judge climbs the ladder of rank that Akaki never leaves, and meets death just as alone at the top of it.
Early Dostoevsky in Gogol’s Petersburg: another solitary man in the city, over four summer nights where Akaki has one winter one.
An English clerk comedy fifty years on: Charles Pooter at his desk in the City, teased by the juniors and delighted by small possessions.
Written the same decade: another story in which a ghost at night teaches a comfortable man to listen to the people below him.
